title: Why not just buy the cheapest?
principle: Pick a few good suppliers for quality, and push them to improve.

screens.text: Let me tell you about a Chennai company. General Motors, the American carmaker, had factories making radiator caps, small parts that stop engines getting too hot. In 1992 GM sold them to Sundram Fasteners. Sundram became GM's main cap supplier, and its Supplier of the Year from 1996 to 2000.

screens.prompt: GM could buy caps from many companies. Why do you think it bought so many from one?

options.label: Its caps cost less than caps from other firms
Its caps worked well year after year
GM had no other firms selling those caps

screens.why: The caps worked well year after year. A radiator cap costs little, but if it fails, the engine can get too hot. Sundram won Supplier of the Year five times in a row, which shows how it kept GM's trust.

screens.title: Deming's rule 4
screens.text: Here's the idea behind that. W. Edwards Deming, an American quality expert, told managers: don't buy on price alone, because a cheap part that fails costs more. Work with a few good suppliers for years, and help them improve. It was rule 4 of his 14 rules.

screens.title: Now look at your bakery
screens.text: Your home bakery is five years old. It's October. Each week, you buy cream from the cheapest of five shops, so the cream keeps changing. Some weeks it won't get thick when you whip it, and cakes fail. Last Holi, your only milk shop also closed for three days.

screens.prompt: Cheap cream saves ₹200 a week. But 2 cakes fail each week, and baking each again costs ₹400. Are you saving money?

options.label: No, you spend ₹600 more each week

screens.why: Exactly. Baking 2 failed cakes again costs 2 × ₹400 = ₹800 a week. Take away the ₹200 saved, and you spend ₹600 more each week. That's Deming's rule: a low buying price does not always mean a low total cost.

wrong.a: That's the price tag. But 2 failed cakes × ₹400 = ₹800 a week. ₹800 minus the ₹200 you saved means you lose ₹600 a week.
wrong.b: Let's check. You save ₹200, but lose 2 × ₹400 = ₹800 on failed cakes. That's ₹600 a week worse, not even.

screens.prompt: Your sister says: buy cream from all five shops. Your cousin says: only the best one. Your friend says: the best two. Who's right?

options.label: Your cousin: only the best one

screens.why: Right. Five shops mean your cream keeps changing. But one shop is also risky. In 1997, a fire at Aisin, the factory making almost all of Toyota's brake valves, stopped Toyota's car factories in Japan for days. So choose a few good suppliers, not just one.

wrong.a: With five shops, your cream keeps changing, and none gets much work from you. With two good shops, both get regular orders and have a reason to keep you happy.
wrong.c: Close. Deming wanted few suppliers, but one is risky. Remember Holi, when your only milk shop closed. In 1997, a fire at Aisin, which made almost all of Toyota's brake valves, stopped Toyota's car factories in Japan for days. Keep a second good shop.

screens.prompt: You now buy from two good shops. But one shop's cream still fails about twice a month. What should you do first?

options.label: Pay him less for bad cream

screens.why: Exactly. Choosing good suppliers is only the first step; you must also push them to improve. Show what went wrong, tell him how thick and fresh the cream must be, and check it together. When a supplier knows what you need, he can work towards it.

wrong.b: A new shop starts from zero, and may be worse. First show this one a failed cake, and tell him what good cream means for you. Push a good supplier before you drop one.
wrong.c: Paying less won't fix his cream. Show him the failed cakes, and agree on what good cream means, so he knows what to fix.

screens.prompt: Even good suppliers tempt you. Your butter shop offers 45 kg at ₹480 a kg, ₹20 off. You use 15 kg monthly. The catch?

options.label: The shop might close for Diwali

screens.why: Exactly. 45 kg × ₹480 = ₹21,600, paid now, for three months of butter. You save ₹900, but much of that cash sits in your fridge for weeks, when Diwali needs it. Remember frozen cash from Unit 1: money tied up in stock can't pay a bill.

wrong.a: You do save 45 × ₹20 = ₹900. But you pay 45 × ₹480 = ₹21,600 now, for butter you'll use over three months. That's frozen cash from Unit 1.
wrong.b: If the shop closes, your second good shop covers you. The real catch is the cash: 45 × ₹480 = ₹21,600 paid now, for three months of butter, just before Diwali.

screens.setup: It's late October. Your best cream shop says it will close for five days during Diwali. That week, you need 30 kg of cream for about 50 cakes. Your second good shop cannot supply enough.
screens.question: How do you make sure you have good cream at Diwali?

options.label: Buy cream from the cheapest shops that week
options.outcome: The cheap cream won't become thick when you whip it on the busiest day of the year. 8 cakes fail, costing ₹3,200 to bake again. Four orders reach families late, and two families complain in the colony WhatsApp group.
options.why: You were back to buying on price alone, on the week you could least afford a failed cake.
options.better: Test new shops before Diwali, and keep the best as a third supplier.

options.label: Test cream from three new shops before Diwali
options.outcome: You try cream from three new shops, making two cakes with each shop's cream. One shop's cream whips well every time, and it can supply 30 kg. It covers Diwali week. No cakes fail, and you keep this shop as your backup.
options.why: Exactly. You chose on quality and tested before you needed it, which took away the risk of a new shop. Now you have a few strong suppliers, not one.

options.label: Ask your best shop for extra cream early
options.outcome: The shop delivers a week's cream before it closes. By day four, some cream has gone bad. You throw away 6 kg and bake 2 cakes again. You manage, but only just.
options.why: Getting it early saved the week, but fresh cream doesn't keep well, and you'll face the same problem every holiday.
options.better: Test new shops before Diwali, and keep the best as a third supplier.

screens.text: You buy flour from whoever is ___ each week, and the flour keeps changing. Deming would say: buy from a ___ good suppliers.
screens.why: Exactly. Buying on price alone brings a different flour every week. A few good suppliers, kept for years and pushed to improve, bring the same good flour every week.

summary: Deming's rule 4: stop buying on the price tag alone. A cheap part can cost the most.
Work with a few strong suppliers for years, and push them to get better.
Keep a few, not one: if your only supplier stops, so do you.

cards.front: Cheap flour saves ₹150 a week, but 2 batches of bread fail at ₹300 each. Is it cheaper?
cards.back: 2 × ₹300 = ₹600 lost, minus ₹150 saved = ₹450 worse. Don't buy on price alone.

cards.front: How many suppliers for one key item?
cards.back: Few enough that each cares about you, more than one so a fire or a holiday can't stop you.

cards.front: A good supplier's goods fail now and then. What first?
options: Show them what failed, and agree a standard
cards.back: Pick good suppliers, then push them to get better.

sources.label: The bolts and nuts of enterprise (Madras Musings)
